subChunks.title: Self Join and CROSS JOIN
subChunks.hookHtml: A table can join to itself. This sounds paradoxical — but it is the only way to compare rows within the same table, or represent hierarchical data.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Self join — comparing rows in one table

-- Find pairs of apprentices where one has more than double the xp of the other:
SELECT a.name AS low, b.name AS high, a.xp, b.xp AS b_xp
FROM   apprentices AS a
JOIN   apprentices AS b ON b.xp > a.xp * 2;

A self join requires two aliases for the same table (a and b) so the engine knows which copy each column comes from.

Hierarchical data (manager → employee)

-- An employee table where manager_id references another employee's id:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM   employees AS e
LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON e.manager_id = m.id;

CROSS JOIN — every combination

SELECT a.name, b.name
FROM apprentices AS a
CROSS JOIN apprentices AS b
WHERE a.id != b.id;  -- exclude self-pairing

CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product — every row from A paired with every row from B. With 6 apprentices that is 36 rows (or 30 excluding self-pairs). Use deliberately and sparingly — it can produce enormous result sets.

storyBeats.text: The tournament board shows every possible apprentice pairing. Both columns list names from the same ledger.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: A self join joins a table to itself using two different aliases. You need two names for the same ledger so you can treat them as distinct sources. CROSS JOIN is every row from the left paired with every row from the right — powerful and dangerous in equal measure.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain when you would use a self join and what the two aliases represent. Also explain what a Cartesian product is.

questions.prompt: What is required to write a self join?
options: Two different aliases for the same table so each copy can be referenced independently
Two copies of the table in the database
questions.answer: Two different aliases for the same table so each copy can be referenced independently
questions.explanation: A self join is just a regular join where both sides reference the same table but with different aliases (e.g. a and b). The aliases let you distinguish which row is which in the ON condition and SELECT list.

questions.prompt: In `employees AS e LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON e.manager_id = m.id`, what does the result row look like for the CEO who has no manager?
options: CEO's name appears with NULL in the manager column
CEO's row is excluded from the result
CEO appears twice — once as employee and once as manager
questions.answer: CEO's name appears with NULL in the manager column
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left side (employees). The CEO has no matching row on the right side (no manager), so the manager column is NULL.

questions.prompt: CROSS JOIN of a 10-row table with a 15-row table returns how many rows?
questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN (Cartesian product) pairs every row from the left with every row from the right: 10 × 15 = 150 rows.

options: When you genuinely need every combination — e.g. generating a calendar grid or a size × colour product matrix
Whenever you need to join two tables without a shared key
As a faster alternative to INNER JOIN
When the tables are too large for INNER JOIN to handle
questions.answer: When you genuinely need every combination — e.g. generating a calendar grid or a size × colour product matrix
questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN is appropriate only when every combination is meaningful by design. Applied accidentally to large tables it produces millions of rows. It is not a substitute for a missing join condition.
